strengths: Novel empirical insight demonstrating MOTR's hidden detection capability (6.3 mAP improvement without track queries), well-grounded through consistent analysis across epochs and datasets

Systematic and thorough ablation studies examining four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposals), providing valuable insights beyond the main method
Fully end-to-end, detector-free approach that avoids external model dependencies and domain gap issues, while achieving highest association quality (59.3 AssA) among end-to-end methods on DanceTrack

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with detailed ablations on proposal sources, thresholds, and data scaling; honest analysis of detection-association conflict reduction (Table 9: 6.3→0.3 mAP drop)

Practical efficiency design with only 17% runtime overhead despite dual decoder passes, including decoder-depth analysis (Fig. 5) showing early saturation for practitioners to optimize speed-accuracy trade-off
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective visualizations and reproducible implementation details
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is recognizing MOTR can generate internal proposals rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; proposal generation uses standard techniques (confidence thresholding + learned anchors)

Modest and dataset-dependent performance gains: DanceTrack shows 69.2 HOTA (slightly below CO-MOT's 69.4) despite higher AssA; MOT17 shows essentially zero improvement over baseline (57.5 vs 57.8 MOTR, significantly below CO-MOT 60.1 and MOTRv3 60.2), raising questions about generality

Severely limited scope: only instantiated on MOTR backbone with acknowledged untested integration into stronger architectures (CO-MOT, MOTRv3); generalization beyond MOTR remains unclear and unstudied

Weak MOT17 results contradict main contribution: on the traditional pedestrian tracking benchmark, the method shows no improvement over baseline and underperforms recent methods. The explanation (detector-sensitive) undermines robustness claims

Incomplete mechanistic analysis of detection-association conflict: paper demonstrates existence but lacks deep explanation of root causes (query-space competition, supervision imbalance, architectural bottlenecks); analysis of why track queries suppress detection is superficial
Non-negligible computational overhead (17% slowdown: 24.8→20.7 FPS) not justified by marginal performance gains, particularly problematic for real-time tracking applications
Hyperparameters under-explored: proposal confidence threshold effects shown but N_learned=10 fixed anchors and λ_prop=0.5 weight not ablated or justified
Comparison fairness issues: gray-font entries in Table 4 indicate different backbone architectures/pretraining across methods, making isolated assessment of self-proposal contribution difficult

strengths: Clear problem identification with empirical evidence (Figure 2) showing detection-association conflict in joint decoding
Comprehensive experimental analysis with four prior injection strategies systematically compared and extensive ablations on multiple datasets
State-of-the-art results on BFT (71.1 HOTA) and best end-to-end on AnimalTrack (45.5 HOTA) with strong DanceTrack performance (69.2 HOTA, highest AssA)
Insightful Track Attention Mass diagnostic analysis inspired by attention sink phenomena in LLMs, with layer-wise and entropy studies
Elegant detector-free design that generates proposals internally, avoiding external model dependencies while maintaining end-to-end purity
Computational efficiency through shallow decoder analysis showing saturation at 2-3 layers with modest runtime overhead (20.7 vs 24.8 FPS)
Well-written paper with clear motivation, good figures, comprehensive implementation details, and thorough ablations supporting design choices
Practical solution to query interference that substantially reduces detection-association conflict (AP drop from -6.3 to -0.3)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: separating detection and tracking passes is a relatively straightforward design choice; TAM analysis is diagnostic rather than prescriptive and doesn't lead to new architectural innovations

Significant generalization weakness on MOT17: 57.5 HOTA (below MOTR baseline at 57.8), even with tuning reaches only 58.4 HOTA vs MOTRv3 (60.2) and CO-MOT (60.1), large gap vs non-end-to-end methods (best 67.5)
Dataset-specific tuning requirements: different training configurations per dataset (clip length 5 vs 3), MOT17 needs hyperparameter changes, undermines generality claims
Marginal improvement over concurrent CO-MOT on main benchmark: 69.2 vs 69.4 HOTA on DanceTrack with both being end-to-end methods, raising questions about practical significance

Incomplete performance attribution: gains decompose into self proposals (+7.0) and data augmentation/CrowdHuman (+6.1), making it unclear how much improvement stems from core decoupling vs training tricks

Track Attention Mass analysis limitations: shows dataset-dependent optimal values (0.4-0.7), connection between entropy and performance assumed but not rigorously proven, analysis is correlative not causative

Missing comparisons and ablations: no identical-setup comparison with CO-MOT (concurrent work), limited failure case analysis for MOT17, no cross-dataset generalization tests, insufficient sensitivity analysis for proposal threshold

Technical gaps: why is self-proposal DetA (80.9) lower than CO-MOT (82.1) despite claimed better internal alignment? Why are learned anchors fixed at 10? Why does CrowdHuman benefit self proposals more? Underexplored explanations
